lesson.title: Relative Clauses & Connectors
lesson.subtitle: die, dat, wie, wat — choosing the relative pronoun by the noun

hook.title: Die for De, Dat for Het
hook.content: Dutch relative pronouns follow the noun: de man die komt, het boek dat ik lees. For people you can also use wie; for an unnamed thing, wat. The relative clause is subordinate, so the verb goes last.

pattern.title: Noun class chooses die or dat
pattern.content: De-words and plurals take die; het-words take dat. De man die hier woont, het boek dat ik lees. The relative clause keeps verb-final order.
pattern.linguist_note: Die and dat are demonstrative forms reused as relatives; English that/which/who divides the work differently.
pattern.trap_note: Do not use dat for a de-word: de man dat is wrong. Check the noun's article first.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Relative Clauses & Connectors):
exercises.target_answer: die, dat, wie, wat, het boek, de man
exercises.meaning: that; which; those, that (conjunction; relative), who, what, book, man
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Relative Clauses & Connectors": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “The man who lives here is my brother.”?
options: De man die hier woont, is mijn broer.
De man dat hier woont, is mijn broer.
De man die hier woont is mijn broer die.
exercises.target_answer: De man die hier woont, is mijn broer.
exercises.meaning: The man who lives here is my brother.
exercises.explanation: “De man die hier woont, is mijn broer.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Relative Clauses & Connectors”.

exercises.idea: The book that I read is good.
cues: The pattern: Noun class chooses die or dat
It means: The book that I read is good.
idea_parts: The book that I read is good.
exercises.target_answer: Het boek dat ik lees, is goed.
exercises.meaning: The book that I read is good.
exercises.explanation: “Het boek dat ik lees, is goed.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Noun class chooses die or dat.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Do not use dat for a de-word: de man dat is wrong. Check the noun's article first.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
options: not Who that says, has right.
exercises.explanation: “Wie dat zegt, heeft recht.” is word-for-word “Who that says, has right.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Noun class chooses die or dat.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: What you say is good.
exercises.explanation: “Wat je zegt, is goed.” reuses only material taught in “Relative Clauses & Connectors” — Noun class chooses die or dat.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Wat je zegt, is goed.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Noun class chooses die or dat.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “The woman who works there is my sister.”
twist.target_answer: De vrouw die daar werkt, is mijn zus.
twist.explanation: Vrouw is a de-word, so the relative pronoun is die; werkt closes the relative clause.

summary.outcome: Choose die or dat by the noun and keep the relative clause verb-final.
summary.takeaway: The noun's article decides the relative pronoun; the clause keeps subordinate order.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Relative Clause Gym.

die.context_phrase: De man die komt, is hier.
die.context_translation: The man who comes is here.
die.etymology_derivation: The de/plural relative pronoun; het takes dat.

dat.etymology_derivation: The neutral demonstrative and conjunction; also the het-relative pronoun.

wie.etymology_derivation: English who is the same question word.

wat.etymology_derivation: English what is the same question word.

boek.etymology_derivation: English book and Dutch boek share the spelling bridge; Dutch oe is /u/.

man.etymology_derivation: The same word as English man.
